title: AI in the Workplace: What Changes When AI Becomes a Coworker?
description: 75-minute facilitated workplace AI session with individual judgment, pair comparison, team redesign, whole-class challenge, and completion of the AI in the Workplace discussion.

steps.label: 🗳️ COLD OPEN
steps.title: Would You Let AI Do This?
choices: AI writes a routine customer email
AI screens 500 résumés and recommends the top 20
AI summarizes a meeting and creates everyone’s action items
AI recommends which employee should receive a promotion
steps.studentTask: Individually select the workplace tasks you would let AI help with. Then be ready to explain where your comfort changes.
steps.roomInstruction: YES · MAYBE · NO — WHERE DOES YOUR TRUST CHANGE?
steps.visualCaption: What changes between a routine email and a promotion decision?

runbook.say: Do not overthink this yet. I want your first instinct. Which of these would you let AI help do at work—and where does your comfort start to change?
runbook.askNext: What changed between the first task and the fourth?
runbook.watchFor: Consequence, fairness, sensitive information, context, accountability, explainability, reversibility, and human judgment.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have responded and you have heard at least two different boundaries.
runbook.landHere: The interesting workplace question is not 'Will AI replace people?' It is: which parts of work should AI do, which parts should humans do, and who is responsible when the system gets it wrong?
runbook.transition: Now let’s name what AI is actually changing at work.

steps.label: ⚙️ MINI-LESSON
steps.title: AI Is Changing Tasks, Not Just Jobs
steps.lead: AI can generate, summarize, analyze, recommend, automate—and increasingly take actions through agents.
steps.studentTask: Listen for the difference between what AI can execute and what humans still need to own.
steps.roomInstruction: AI CAN DO MORE. HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY DOES NOT DISAPPEAR.
steps.visualCaption: If everyone has AI, what makes one employee more valuable than another?

runbook.say: AI is moving from answering questions toward doing pieces of work: drafting, summarizing, analyzing, recommending, automating, and increasingly acting through agents. But somebody still has to define the real problem, provide context, judge quality, handle exceptions, understand consequences, and take responsibility.
runbook.askNext: If everyone has access to AI, what makes one employee more valuable than another?
runbook.watchFor: Domain knowledge, judgment, communication, problem framing, creativity, verification, adaptability, relationships, and accountability.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students have generated several human-value ideas but before you resolve the question.
runbook.landHere: AI literacy at work is not just tool use. It is knowing what to delegate, what to verify, and what humans must still own.
runbook.transition: Let’s make that personal. Pick a job you may actually have.

steps.label: 🧠 INDEPENDENT
steps.title: My Future Job Audit
steps.lead: Choose a realistic job you might want in the next 3–5 years.
steps.studentTask: Write your job + five tasks. Classify each: 🤖 AI could mostly do this · 🤝 Human + AI should do this together · 🧠 Human should remain primarily responsible. For each, note why, what could go wrong if AI handled too much, and what human skill adds value. Submit one task where human judgment matters most.
steps.roomInstruction: MY JOB → 5 TASKS → AI / HUMAN+AI / HUMAN
steps.visualCaption: Are you protecting a task because humans truly add value—or because that is how the job has always been done?

runbook.say: Work independently first. I want your own judgment before anyone else influences it.
runbook.askNext: Are you protecting this task because a human really adds value—or because this is how the job has always been done?
runbook.watchFor: Students keeping all interesting work human while automating only boring work. Push them to distinguish preference from responsibility.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have identified five tasks and one task where human judgment matters most.
runbook.landHere: AI may remove, shrink, or reshape tasks without eliminating the human role. The human role often shifts toward judgment, exception handling, relationships, and accountability.
runbook.transition: Now find someone whose future work looks different from yours.

steps.label: 👥 PAIR COMPARE
steps.title: Find One Disagreement
steps.lead: Compare where AI helps vs. where humans remain critical.
steps.studentTask: Pair with someone in a different area if possible. Find one task where you disagree about how much AI should do. Each person gets about two minutes to defend the choice.
steps.roomInstruction: FIND ONE TASK YOU DISAGREE ABOUT
steps.visualCaption: What evidence or consequence changes your answer?

runbook.say: Do not look for agreement. Find one boundary where your judgments differ.
runbook.askNext: What consequence, stakeholder, or missing context explains the disagreement?
runbook.watchFor: Students realizing that the same AI capability can be acceptable in one context and risky in another.
runbook.advanceWhen: Pairs have identified one disagreement and 2–3 examples have been shared aloud.
runbook.landHere: There is rarely one universal answer to 'should AI do this?' Context and consequence matter.
runbook.transition: Now scale that thinking up from one task to an entire job.

steps.label: 🛠️ TEAM CHALLENGE
steps.title: Redesign the Job
steps.lead: It is 2028. Your organization has powerful AI tools and agents.
steps.studentTask: Teams of 3–5: choose a role. Build a Human + AI Job Design with three columns: AI DOES · HUMAN DOES · HUMAN CHECKS. Then answer: 1) What task disappears or shrinks? 2) What human skill becomes more valuable? 3) Where must a human have override authority? 4) What is one thing you would explicitly NOT automate? Submit your one-sentence redesign.
steps.roomInstruction: AI DOES · HUMAN DOES · HUMAN CHECKS
steps.visualCaption: Maximum useful AI without irresponsible automation.

runbook.say: Your goal is not to protect the old version of the job. Redesign it. Get maximum value from AI without giving away responsibility.
runbook.askNext: What is the one thing your team would explicitly NOT automate—and why?
runbook.watchFor: Vague 'a human checks it' answers. Ask exactly what the human verifies, what evidence they need, and whether they can override the system.
runbook.advanceWhen: Each team has all three columns, the three required answers, and one explicit non-automation boundary.
runbook.landHere: Human oversight only matters when it is specific and when the human has authority to question, correct, or override.

steps.label: 🎤 SHARE + CHALLENGE
steps.title: Defend Your Redesign
steps.lead: 60–90 seconds per team. Then the room gets one challenge.
steps.studentTask: Pitch: “We redesigned the role of ____. AI handles ____. Humans remain responsible for ____ because ____.” After each pitch, another student asks: “What could go wrong?” The presenting team must answer with one safeguard.
steps.visualCaption: What could go wrong—and what would you put in place to prevent it?

runbook.say: Keep the pitch short. I care less about the polish and more about whether your boundary makes sense.
runbook.watchFor: Whether safeguards actually respond to the risk: review, appeal, documentation, transparency, training, privacy protection, human override.
runbook.advanceWhen: Several teams have defended their redesign and the class has challenged assumptions.
runbook.landHere: A responsible workplace design connects productivity gains to safeguards for the people affected.
runbook.transition: You have now done almost all of the thinking your discussion post needs.

steps.label: ✍️ DISCUSSION SPRINT
steps.title: Turn Today’s Work Into Your Initial Post
steps.lead: Do not start from scratch. Reuse your Job Audit + Team Challenge reasoning.
steps.studentTask: Open Canvas → Discussion / Activity | AI in the Workplace. Submit your initial post using one specific workplace scenario. Include: Workplace Task → AI Assistance → Worker Impact → Organizational Risk → Responsible Workplace Practice; at least two perspectives; one benefit; one risk/limitation; one responsible action; and a closing question.
steps.visualCaption: Specific scenario · pathway · 2 perspectives · benefit · risk · responsible action · closing question

runbook.say: You already generated the substance. Your job now is to assemble it into the discussion—not invent a new answer.
runbook.askNext: Can a reader clearly see who benefits, who may be disadvantaged, and what the organization should do?
runbook.watchFor: Missing second perspective, generic claims, no responsible action, no closing question.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have submitted the initial post.
runbook.landHere: Strong workplace AI analysis connects the tool to worker impact, organizational risk, and a concrete responsible practice.
runbook.transition: Now use two classmates’ posts to widen your thinking.

steps.label: 💬 TWO REPLIES
steps.title: Complete Both Classmate Responses
steps.lead: Move the conversation forward. Do more than say “I agree.”
steps.studentTask: Submit two replies to two classmates. Each reply should compare, extend, question, or respectfully challenge the reasoning. Use a different move for each reply if possible.

runbook.say: Pick posts that give you something to think about. Your replies should add something the original writer did not already say.
runbook.askNext: What perspective, missing context, risk, safeguard, or human-judgment question can you add?
runbook.watchFor: Replies that merely praise or repeat the original post.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have completed both replies.
runbook.landHere: Multiple perspectives change what responsible workplace practice looks like.
runbook.transition: Let’s close on the question we left hanging earlier.

steps.label: 🏁 DEBRIEF + EXIT
steps.title: If Everyone Has AI, What Makes You Valuable?
steps.lead: Your advantage will not simply be access to AI.
steps.studentTask: Finish all three: 1) AI will probably change my future work by ____. 2) One skill I need to strengthen because of AI is ____. 3) One workplace decision I would not allow AI to make alone is ____ because ____.
steps.visualCaption: What do humans still need to know, judge, and own?

runbook.say: Your competitive advantage probably is not going to be that you can use AI. Everyone will be expected to use AI. Your advantage will be knowing what to delegate to it, how to judge what comes back, and when the human needs to take control.
runbook.askNext: What human skill becomes more valuable—not less valuable—because AI is everywhere?
runbook.watchFor: Knowing what questions to ask, domain expertise, critical thinking, communication, creativity, verification, understanding people, ethical judgment, knowing when not to use AI, adaptability, accountability.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students have submitted the three-part exit response.
runbook.landHere: AI literacy in the workplace is the ability to use AI without giving away human responsibility.
runbook.transition: You should leave with the discussion completed and a clearer picture of your own future work.
